title: Problem 21
statement_text: Is there an infinite family $\mathcal{G}$ of finite graphs, not containing cliques or independent sets, such that for all $H\in\mathcal{G}$, there is no finite $H$-induced-saturated graph?
context_text: A graph $G$ (on at least two vertices) is $H$-induced-saturated if it has no induced copy of $H$ but perturbing any pair (deleting an edge or adding a non-edge) creates an induced copy of $H$. No such graph exists when $H$ is a clique or an independent set on more than two vertices, and Martin and Smith showed there is no finite $P_4$-induced-saturated graph; finite $P_t$-induced-saturated graphs exist iff $t\ne1,4$. The authors prove that every finite graph $H$ that is not a clique or an independent set admits a countably infinite $H$-induced-saturated graph, and even one such that every locally finite perturbation (toggling a nonempty set of pairs with every vertex in finitely many of them) creates an induced copy of $H$. In the finite case the classification is widely open: besides $P_4$, cliques and independent sets, no finite graph $H$ is known to have no finite $H$-induced-saturated graph, so it is asked whether there are infinitely many non-trivial such $H$.

title: Problem 22
statement_text: For a finite graph $H$ and integer $n$, let $G_{H,n}$ denote the graph with the $H$-free graphs on vertex set $[n]$ as vertices, and with an edge between $G,G^{\prime}\in V(G_{H,n})$ if and only if $|E(G)\triangle E(G^{\prime})|=1$. For which $H$ is $G_{H,n}$ disconnected for all sufficiently large $n$?
context_text: A graph $G$ (on at least two vertices) is $H$-induced-saturated if it has no induced copy of $H$ but perturbing any pair (deleting an edge or adding a non-edge) creates an induced copy of $H$. No such graph exists when $H$ is a clique or an independent set on more than two vertices, and Martin and Smith showed there is no finite $P_4$-induced-saturated graph; finite $P_t$-induced-saturated graphs exist iff $t\ne1,4$. Here $H$-free means having no induced copy of $H$, and $[n]=\{1,\dots,n\}$. An $H$-induced-saturated graph on $[n]$ is exactly an isolated vertex of $G_{H,n}$, so showing that $G_{H,n}$ is disconnected may be easier than finding induced-saturated graphs. Using the inductive definition of cographs, $G_{P_4,n}$ is connected for every $n\ge1$, consistent with the non-existence of finite $P_4$-induced-saturated graphs. The problem was suggested by Torsten Ueckerdt.

title: Problem 23
statement_text: For which finite tournaments $H$, does there exist a countable tournament $G$ that does not contain $H$ as subtournament, yet any tournament obtained from $G$ by changing the direction of a single arc does contain $H$?
context_text: A graph $G$ (on at least two vertices) is $H$-induced-saturated if it has no induced copy of $H$ but perturbing any pair (deleting an edge or adding a non-edge) creates an induced copy of $H$. No such graph exists when $H$ is a clique or an independent set on more than two vertices, and Martin and Smith showed there is no finite $P_4$-induced-saturated graph; finite $P_t$-induced-saturated graphs exist iff $t\ne1,4$. For tournaments, the natural perturbation is reversing the direction of an arc, and $G$ contains $H$ if some subtournament of $G$ is isomorphic to $H$. When $H$ is the directed triangle there is no finite example, but an infinite one exists: the transitive tournament on $\mathbb{Q}$ with $q\to q'$ iff $q<q'$, since reversing an arc $q\to q'$ creates a directed triangle with any $r$ such that $q<r<q'$. When $H$ is the transitive tournament on $3$ vertices, the directed triangle itself is a finite example. The paper settles the analogous question for graphs (a countable example exists iff $H$ is not a clique or an independent set).

title: Conjecture 24
statement_text: Let $T$ be a finite tournament. If $T$ is not transitive, then there exists a countably infinite $T$-free tournament $S_{T}$ such that every locally finite perturbation of $S_{T}$ has an induced copy of $T$.
context_text: Graphs may be countably infinite. A locally finite perturbation of a graph $G$ is obtained by perturbing (toggling) a nonempty, possibly infinite, set of pairs such that every vertex lies in only finitely many perturbed pairs. The paper's main theorem: if a finite graph $H$ is not a clique or an independent set, there is a countably infinite $H$-free graph $G_H$ such that every locally finite perturbation of $G_H$ contains an induced copy of $H$ (in particular $G_H$ is $H$-induced-saturated). For tournaments, perturbing a pair means reversing the arc between them, and a locally finite perturbation reverses a nonempty set of arcs with every vertex in finitely many of them; $T$-free means that no subtournament is isomorphic to $T$, and induced copy means subtournament. The conjecture is proposed as the tournament analogue of the main theorem. Local finiteness forces $S_T$ to be infinite, and the non-transitivity condition is necessary because every tournament on $2^n$ vertices contains a transitive subtournament on $n$ vertices.

title: Conjecture 25
statement_text: Let $k\geq 3$ be an integer, and let $H$ be a finite $k$-uniform hypergraph. If $H$ has both an edge and a non-edge, then there exists a countably infinite $k$-uniform hypergraph $G_{H}$ such that every locally finite perturbation of $G_{H}$ has an induced copy of $H$.
context_text: Graphs may be countably infinite. A locally finite perturbation of a graph $G$ is obtained by perturbing (toggling) a nonempty, possibly infinite, set of pairs such that every vertex lies in only finitely many perturbed pairs. The paper's main theorem: if a finite graph $H$ is not a clique or an independent set, there is a countably infinite $H$-free graph $G_H$ such that every locally finite perturbation of $G_H$ contains an induced copy of $H$ (in particular $G_H$ is $H$-induced-saturated). For a $k$-uniform hypergraph, a single perturbation adds or removes one hyperedge (a $k$-set of vertices), and a locally finite perturbation does this for a nonempty set of $k$-sets with each vertex in finitely many of them; an induced copy of $H$ is a set of $|V(H)|$ vertices whose induced subhypergraph is isomorphic to $H$. The conjecture is called the strongest proposed extension of the main theorem to hypergraphs, and having both an edge and a non-edge is the analogue of not being a clique or independent set. As stated in the paper the conjecture does not explicitly require $G_H$ itself to contain no induced copy of $H$; by analogy with the main theorem this is presumably intended.

title: Conjecture 26
statement_text: Let $k\geq 2$ be an integer, and let $c$ be a $k$-colouring of the edges of a finite clique $K$ such that there is an edge of every colour. Then there is a colouring $\chi$ of the edges of the complete countably infinite graph such that every locally finite perturbation contains a copy of $K$ with colouring $c$.
context_text: Graphs may be countably infinite. A locally finite perturbation of a graph $G$ is obtained by perturbing (toggling) a nonempty, possibly infinite, set of pairs such that every vertex lies in only finitely many perturbed pairs. The paper's main theorem: if a finite graph $H$ is not a clique or an independent set, there is a countably infinite $H$-free graph $G_H$ such that every locally finite perturbation of $G_H$ contains an induced copy of $H$ (in particular $G_H$ is $H$-induced-saturated). For a $k$-colouring of the edges of a (finite or infinite) complete graph, a locally finite perturbation changes the colours on the edges of a nonempty locally finite subgraph (every vertex incident with finitely many recoloured edges). A copy of $K$ with colouring $c$ is a set of $|V(K)|$ vertices on which the colouring is isomorphic to $c$. The requirement that every colour appears in $c$ is the analogue of $H$ being neither a clique nor an independent set (the case $k=2$ with colours edge and non-edge is the main theorem). As stated in the paper the conjecture does not explicitly require $\chi$ itself to contain no copy of $K$ with colouring $c$; by analogy with the main theorem this is presumably intended.
